passage: Sit, Ishita, the chai can wait. You're calling this launch a disaster, and it reminds me of the library project I ran at twenty-five, the first one with my name on top. We set up reading corners in six municipal schools. By the end of the term only two were still being used, and I walked into my manager's cabin ready to say the whole thing had failed. Before I could, I caught the word in my own mouth. Failed? Everything? So I took a sheet and wrote one to ten for each part. Book selection, eight; the children loved the comics. Teacher training, three; we did one session and left. Storage, two; the monsoon soaked the shelves. Mr Dsouza looked at the sheet and said, 'Pema, this is a report, not a funeral.' That sheet became the plan for the next year, and the two corners that worked taught us why the other four didn't. So give me your numbers, part by part.

qa.q: How many municipal schools got reading corners?
qa.a: Reading corners were set up in six municipal schools, and only two were still being used by the end of the term.

qa.q: Why did calling the whole project a failure feel reasonable to Pema at first?
qa.a: Pema was disappointed and embarrassed that four of the six corners had stopped being used, and that loss was so vivid it seemed to colour everything, so 'failed' felt like an honest summary.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed what Pema did next?
qa.a: Pema caught the word 'failed' before saying it and rated each part from one to ten, which showed the book choice worked while training and storage needed fixing.

qa.q: How might Mr Dsouza have seen the project once he looked at the sheet?
qa.a: Mr Dsouza saw a project with real strengths and clear weak spots, not a funeral, and a sheet that could guide the next year's plan.

grounding: An adult about to call a whole project a failure rates each part on a scale instead, and the mixed scores guide the next attempt.

passage: Fifteen minutes before her call with Rafiq, Zainab sat on the steps of the community hall with her phone at four percent. The weekend coding workshop she had planned for a month was over. The projector had died in the first hour, half the borrowed laptops never connected to the wifi, and three parents had left early. She typed 'Honestly, it flopped' into her notes for the call, then stopped. Flopped how much? With no charger and no time, she scribbled on the back of the attendance sheet. Turnout: nine out of ten, twenty-eight of thirty came. Equipment: two. The paper puzzle game she had invented when the screen went dark: eight, because the kids begged for another round. Timing: five. When Rafiq called, she read out the numbers instead of the word. 'So the teaching worked and the tech didn't,' he said. 'Book the hall again. We'll bring our own router.'

qa.q: How many of the thirty children came to the workshop?
qa.a: Twenty-eight of thirty came to the workshop.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when she typed 'Honestly, it flopped'?
qa.a: She was deflated and frustrated after the projector and laptops failed, so those breakdowns felt like the whole story of the weekend.

qa.q: What small step helped Zainab under time pressure, and why did it work?
qa.a: Scoring each part quickly on the attendance sheet split the day into pieces, showing the teaching and turnout were strong while only the equipment needed fixing.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see the workshop after hearing the numbers?
qa.a: Rafiq sees a workshop worth repeating, where the teaching worked and only the tech needs a fix, so he tells her to book the hall again.

grounding: Under time pressure, an adult stops herself from summing up a whole event as a flop and rates each part, turning a verdict into a plan.

passage: The lights came up in the small auditorium in Koramangala and Mridul was already on his feet, heading for the door. On the pavement outside he told Charu, 'Eight months of weekends, and it's garbage. Everyone heard that hum.' Charu, who had shared a flat with him since college, pulled a pen and a crumpled bill from her bag. 'Fine. Garbage out of ten?' He almost laughed. Then, slowly, he started. The hum in the second half, a three. The interviews with the old tailors, a nine; one woman in the front row had wiped her eyes. The edit dragged in the middle, maybe a five. The ending, seven. He looked at the bill. It didn't say garbage anywhere. 'The sound can be fixed,' he said. 'The tailors can't be found again.' They walked to the bus stop arguing about where to borrow a better microphone.

qa.q: Which part of the film did Mridul rate a nine?
qa.a: He rated the interviews with the old tailors a nine.

qa.q: Why did calling the film garbage feel true to Mridul as he left the auditorium?
qa.a: He was embarrassed that everyone had heard the hum, and after eight months of weekends that one flaw felt so loud it swallowed everything else.

qa.q: What did Charu's question achieve that arguing with Mridul would not?
qa.a: Asking 'Garbage out of ten?' got him to score the parts himself, so he found the strong interviews and the fixable sound on his own instead of being told.

qa.q: What is it like for Charu to hear her flatmate call eight months of work garbage?
qa.a: Charu is likely concerned for him but doesn't argue; she offers a way to look again and then happily plans the microphone with him.

grounding: A young adult who calls a whole film worthless rates its parts on a scale and finds what can be kept and what can be fixed.

passage: Salma unzipped her bag in the classroom and her stomach dropped. The maths notebook was still on the dining table at home. Ramesh Sir checked homework right after prayer. He'll shout in front of everyone, she thought. Maybe he'll hit my hands with the ruler. Then he'll send me to the principal. The principal will call Ammi, and Ammi will cry, and they'll say I can't come back to this school. Everyone will remember me as the girl who got thrown out. Her hands were cold when Ramesh Sir reached her desk. 'Forgot it?' he asked. She nodded, eyes stinging. 'Bring it tomorrow and show me first thing,' he said, and moved to the next desk. Salma stared at her empty hands for a long time.

qa.q: What did Salma leave at home?
qa.a: Salma left her maths notebook on the dining table at home.

qa.q: Why did being thrown out of school feel so certain to Salma?
qa.a: She was scared and ashamed, and each imagined step, from shouting to the principal to Ammi crying, seemed to follow from the one before, so the fear felt like fact.

qa.q: What could Salma try the next time her mind races ahead like this?
qa.a: She could ask herself what usually happens when someone forgets homework, and remember that Ramesh Sir only asked her to bring it the next day.

qa.q: How might Ramesh Sir see the forgotten notebook?
qa.a: To him it is a small, ordinary slip, which is why he simply asks for it first thing tomorrow and moves on.

grounding: A child who forgot homework imagines a chain from shouting and a ruler to being expelled, while the real response is small.

passage:
Sunday night. Mahima sat up in bed. The science worksheet! It was still blank in her bag. Miss Joshi would shout. She might hit her palm with the ruler. Then the principal would expel her, and the whole colony would know. When her big brother Kamal came to switch off the light, she was shaking. 'Tell Miss first thing,' he said. 'I'll walk you in.'
Monday. Mahima whispered it at the staffroom door. Miss Joshi only said, 'Wednesday, then,' and went back to her tea.
Thursday. Mahima reached for her library book and found it missing. Her chest fluttered. Then she thought of Monday. 'One book,' she told herself. 'Not the end of everything.'

qa.q: On which day did Mahima tell Miss Joshi about the worksheet?
qa.a: She whispered it at the staffroom door on Monday.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling on Sunday night, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was terrified; she sat up, pictured the ruler and being expelled, and was shaking when Kamal came in, because each worse picture felt real.

qa.q: Which step helped break the chain of worst endings?
qa.a: Kamal's plan to tell Miss Joshi first thing, and walking in with her, let Mahima see the real result, a new deadline, which she remembered on Thursday.

qa.q: How does Kamal see his sister's fear?
qa.a: Kamal takes her fear seriously enough to offer to walk her in, while treating the worksheet as a small problem that speaking up can fix.

grounding: A child's forgotten worksheet grows into imagined scolding, punishment and expulsion, and over a few days the real small outcome shrinks the leap.

subtype: One wrong answer means being sent away [Actor]
passage: Jaya, stop crying over one forgotten notebook and listen to your old granny. When I was eight, at the convent school in Shillong, I left my copybook on the kitchen shelf. Walking to school, I built the whole disaster in my head. Sister Agnes would scold me in front of the class. She would rap my knuckles. She would send a letter home, and I would be sent away to some far school, and everyone would whisper 'that Elizabeth' for the rest of my life. By the gate I was sobbing. And do you know what happened? Sister Agnes looked at my face, not at my hands. 'Child, it's one copybook,' she said. 'Bring it tomorrow.' I was so surprised I stopped crying mid-hiccup. I still think of that walk when my mind runs ahead of me, and it still does, even now, with all this grey hair.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth leave on the kitchen shelf?
qa.a: She left her copybook on the kitchen shelf.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth's imagined disaster feel so real on that walk?
qa.a: She was frightened and ashamed, and each picture, from the scolding to being sent away, led to a worse one, so by the gate the fear felt like certainty.

qa.q: What turning point in the story broke the chain of worst outcomes?
qa.a: Sister Agnes looking at her face and saying it was one copybook showed the real outcome was small, and that surprise stopped the spiral.

qa.q: How might Sister Agnes have seen the sobbing girl at the gate?
qa.a: She probably saw a frightened child whose fear was far bigger than the mistake, which is why she answered the face, not the forgotten book.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a child, one forgotten copybook grew into imagined scolding, punishment and being sent away forever.

passage: Afreen, put the phone down for a minute. You've checked it twenty times since dinner. Let your Farhan Mamu tell you something. When I was fifteen, there were no chats, just the landline in the corridor. I called my best friend Vinod on a Sunday about the cricket match, and his mother said he'd call back. He didn't. Monday, nothing. By Tuesday I had it all worked out: he was angry about the run-out, he'd told the whole team, they'd all laughed at me, and I would be dropped and friendless for the rest of school. I skipped practice so no one could say it to my face. On Wednesday Vinod turned up at our door, soaked. The rain had killed their phone line for three days. He'd been worried I was angry with him! Every step of my story had felt certain, and not one of them had happened.

qa.q: Why had Vinod not called back?
qa.a: The rain had killed their phone line for three days.

qa.q: Why did Farhan feel sure the whole team was laughing at him?
qa.a: He was anxious and hurt when Vinod didn't call, and each fearful guess, the run-out, the team, being dropped, felt like the next logical step, so fear passed for certainty.

qa.q: What choice in the story made things worse, and what could have helped instead?
qa.a: Skipping practice kept the fear untested; walking over to Vinod's house or asking a teammate would have shown the truth days sooner.

qa.q: What was the silence like from Vinod's side?
qa.a: Vinod was cut off by the dead line and was worried Farhan was angry with him, so he came over in the rain to check.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a teenager, an unreturned call grew into certainty that the friendship was over and everyone was mocking him.

passage: The overnight bus to Nagpur had crossed into forest, and Urmila's phone showed one grey tick. Two hours earlier she had sent Anjali the voice note: the long, shaky one about the boy from tuition. Still one tick. Still nothing. By the third hour she had it figured out. Anjali had heard it and cringed. She had forwarded it to the group. That was why the group had gone silent too. On Monday they would all look away when she walked in. Urmila pressed her forehead to the cold window, rehearsing how she would eat lunch alone. At a dhaba stop near dawn, three bars flickered up. Messages poured in. Anjali: 'Sorry!! Phone was taken away for mock test week 🙏 Call me the second you're back, I need to hear EVERYTHING.'

qa.q: Where was Urmila while she waited for Anjali's reply?
qa.a: She was on the overnight bus to Nagpur, which had crossed into forest.

qa.q: Why did Urmila's story about the group feel certain to her?
qa.a: She felt exposed and afraid after sending such a personal voice note, so the silence seemed to confirm her fear, and each guess felt like proof of the next.

qa.q: What could Urmila tell herself the next time a reply is slow?
qa.a: She could list other reasons, like no network or a busy friend, notice that one grey tick means it wasn't even delivered, and wait for facts before planning Monday.

qa.q: How would Anjali probably feel if she knew about Urmila's night?
qa.a: Anjali would likely feel sorry that her friend suffered for hours, since she was eager to hear everything and had simply lost her phone for the week.

grounding: A teenager on a long bus ride turns a friend's silence into certainty that the friendship is over and the whole group knows.

passage: Madhav sat on the stairwell of their building in Dadar, where the signal was best, and stared at the word under his message: Seen. He had sent Damini a birthday wish at seven, with the song from the school play they had both been in. It was now nine-thirty. She'd seen it and said nothing. So the song was cringe. So she had shown it to Pooja and Aman and they had laughed. So the three of them had been faking friendship since the play, and tomorrow at the bus stop they would all go quiet when he came. His mother called him up for dinner twice. He ate without speaking. At 10:40 his phone buzzed. 'Sorry sorry, family dinner, twenty-two cousins!! I've played the song four times already 😊 thank you!!'

qa.q: At what time did Madhav send the birthday wish?
qa.a: He sent Damini the birthday wish at seven.

qa.q: Why did the word 'Seen' feel like proof to Madhav?
qa.a: He felt anxious and a little embarrassed about sending a song, so a seen but unanswered message seemed to confirm his fear, and each worse guess felt like the obvious next step.

qa.q: What could Madhav do while waiting that would calm the spiral?
qa.a: He could name other likely reasons, like a birthday dinner, and set the phone aside until morning instead of building the story further.

qa.q: How might his mother read his silence at dinner?
qa.a: She would likely notice he was upset and withdrawn without knowing why, and might wonder what had happened.

grounding: A teenager whose friend has seen but not answered a message concludes, step by step, that she and others were mocking him, until the real reason arrives.

passage: The rejection email arrived while Zanele was queuing for a taxi outside the Braamfontein campus. Thank you for your interest. She read it three times on the ride home. By the time she climbed the stairs to the flat, the logic had built itself. If the engineering firm didn't want her, none of them would. Graduation would come with no job. She'd move back to Soweto and sit in her mother's lounge while the neighbours asked what all that studying had been for. Her little brother, who told everyone his sister would build bridges, would stop saying it. Kaito, her flatmate, found her sitting on the floor with her shoes still on. 'That's one company,' he said, handing her tea. 'How many applications have you still got open?' She counted, frowning. Seven. She hadn't thought of them once all the way home.

qa.q: How many applications did Zanele still have open?
qa.a: She still had seven applications open.

qa.q: Why did Zanele's chain from one rejection to living in shame feel logical to her?
qa.a: She was crushed and ashamed, and each picture seemed to follow from the one before, so she skipped the many steps in between, like the seven other applications.

qa.q: What countermeasure did Kaito's question offer?
qa.a: Asking how many applications were still open made her count real evidence, which interrupted the jump from one no to never being employed.

qa.q: How does Kaito see the rejection?
qa.a: Kaito sees it as one company's decision, not a verdict on her future, and he brings her back to the facts gently with tea and a question.

grounding: A final-year student turns one failed interview into an imagined future of unemployment and family shame, skipping every step in between.

passage: The placement cell corridor still smelled of fresh paint. Irawati sat on the bench outside Room 4, where the panel had just thanked her and called the next name. She had frozen on the second question. Her mind was already running. Six companies were visiting this month and they all talked to each other, surely. Word would spread. Every panel would see a girl who froze. May would come, and her batchmates would post their offer letters while she stayed silent. Her father had told the whole village she would work in Bengaluru. She would have to go home and face him. Rukmini, the placement coordinator, stopped by the bench with a clipboard. 'Your aptitude score was the third best in the batch,' she said. 'Did you know that?' Irawati hadn't even looked.

qa.q: What happened to Irawati in Room 4?
qa.a: She froze on the second question, and the panel thanked her and called the next name.

qa.q: Why did Irawati believe every company would hear about her freezing?
qa.a: She was panicked and ashamed, so the idea that companies talk to each other felt obvious, and each fearful step seemed to prove the next.

qa.q: What could Irawati do to check the chain she had built?
qa.a: She could write down each step and ask what evidence supports it, starting from facts like her strong aptitude score and the other companies still visiting.

qa.q: What does Rukmini's comment show about how others see Irawati?
qa.a: Rukmini sees a strong candidate with the third-best aptitude score, not someone who is finished after one hard interview.

grounding: A final-year student turns one frozen interview answer into imagined rejection by every company and shame at home.

passage:
Subject: I think I've ruined everything

Hafsa di,
You said to write if placements got hard, so here I am at 2 a.m. The analytics firm rejected me today after the final round. I keep replaying it. If I couldn't crack the one company that matches my project, who will take me? I can already see June: everyone joining offices, me refreshing job sites at home. Amma has been telling the relatives that I'm 'almost settled'. She'll have to take that back at the next wedding. Appa won't say anything, which is worse. I know I'm jumping ahead, but it feels like I'm just being realistic. Tell me honestly, did this happen to anyone in your batch? Did they recover?
Sorry for the long mail.
Jahnavi

qa.a: The analytics firm rejected Jahnavi after the final round.

qa.q: How could Hafsa reply in a way that helps?

qa.q: How might Amma see the rejection if Jahnavi told her?
qa.a: Amma might see it as one company's no rather than a failure, and could care more about Jahnavi's worry than about what relatives say.

grounding: In an email to an older student, a final-year student lets one rejection grow into an imagined future of unemployment and family embarrassment.

passage:
Thursday, late
Tarun didn't eat lunch today. He'd found a wrong figure in the quarterly report we sent the client yesterday: one column added twice on page nine. By four o'clock he was saying he'd be fired, that nobody would hire someone who can't add, that he should start looking at jobs back in Indore. His voice had gone thin. I pulled a chair next to his desk and asked, 'Okay. Worst thing that could realistically happen?' He said the client might complain. 'And how likely is that, if you email the correction today?' He thought. 'Low, I guess.' 'And then?' 'Then Meenakshi ma'am asks me to be more careful.' He sent the correction at 4:30. The client replied, 'Thanks for flagging.' I'm writing this down because I nearly just said 'relax', and that would have done nothing.
Vijay

qa.q: What mistake did Tarun find in the report?
qa.a: He found one column added twice on page nine of the quarterly report.

qa.q: What did Vijay feel while watching Tarun, and what shows it?
qa.a: Vijay was concerned, noticing that Tarun skipped lunch and his voice had gone thin, and was relieved enough afterwards to note that saying 'relax' would have done nothing.

qa.q: Why did Vijay's questions work better than 'relax'?
qa.a: Asking for the worst realistic outcome and how likely it was made Tarun check his fear against facts, so the disaster shrank to a simple correction email.

qa.q: Why did being fired feel certain to Tarun?
qa.a: Tarun was ashamed of such a basic error, and that shame made one wrong figure feel like proof he couldn't do the job at all.

grounding: A colleague watches a peer treat a small report error as career-ending and uses calm questions about realistic outcomes and likelihood to shrink the fear.

passage: The agriculture office in Pala shut at five, but Aadhya was still at her desk when Jomon came back for his umbrella. She had the rainfall report open. 'I put Kadanad's figures under Karoor,' she said without looking up. 'It went to the collectorate this morning. They'll think the whole survey is rubbish. There'll be an inquiry. I'll lose the posting.' Jomon hung the umbrella back on the hook and sat on the next desk. 'What's the worst that can actually happen this week?' She took a breath. 'They send it back.' 'How likely is anything worse, for two swapped rows?' 'Not very,' she admitted. 'And if they send it back?' 'Fix the rows. Send it again.' She was already typing the corrected table. Jomon waited till she pressed send, then walked her to the bus stand under his umbrella.

qa.q: What mistake had Aadhya made in the rainfall report?
qa.a: She put Kadanad's figures under Karoor.

qa.q: What does Jomon hanging his umbrella back on the hook suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he was concerned for Aadhya and chose to stay, sensing her fear was far bigger than the mistake.

qa.q: What made Jomon's questions a good countermeasure?
qa.a: He asked for the worst realistic outcome, how likely anything worse was, and what she would do, which turned a feared inquiry into a fix she could make that evening.

qa.q: Why did an inquiry feel certain to Aadhya?
qa.a: Aadhya was alarmed that the report had already gone to the collectorate, so the mistake felt public, and the imagined chain to losing her posting seemed like logic.

subtype: Asking what would I do if [Response]
passage:
Monday. The email said 'restructuring' and 'town hall on Friday', and Avni spent the night scrolling job sites with her heart pounding.
Wednesday. She opened her notebook and made three columns. Feared: I lose my job on Friday. What I'd do: update my CV this week, message two old managers, ask Rafiq to run mock interviews with me. How likely: our team just got a new client, so maybe one in five. She read the second column twice. It was a list of things she could actually do, and her shoulders dropped a little.
Friday. The town hall announced changes to two other departments. Avni's team stayed. She still sent the messages to her old managers that evening. 'Just in case,' she told Rafiq. 'And because I'm not scared of the list anymore.'

qa.q: What did Monday's email mention?
qa.a: It mentioned 'restructuring' and a 'town hall on Friday'.

qa.q: How did Avni feel after reading her second column, and why?
qa.a: She felt calmer and a little relieved, because the list turned vague dread into concrete things she could do, and her shoulders dropped.

qa.q: Why does writing 'what I'd do' help more than only hoping the fear is wrong?
qa.a: A plan gives choices whatever happens, so even if the fear comes true there is a next step, which shrinks helpless dread into options.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see the change in Avni between Monday and Friday?
qa.a: Rafiq probably notices her move from sleepless panic to steady action, and is glad to be part of the plan through the mock interviews.

grounding: An adult writes down the feared outcome, what she could do and how likely it is, and the plan turns dread into manageable options over a week.

subtype: Asking what would I do if [Response]
passage: Anjali, you keep saying 'what if it all goes wrong' about Pune. Your Gurleen Bua knows that song. I was twenty-four when the letter came from the Toronto hospital accounts office. Everyone clapped, and I lay awake. What if I'm alone? What if I fail and come back and the whole mohalla laughs? One night your Dadi found me in the kitchen and gave me a notebook. 'Write it properly,' she said. So I did. At the top: I will be lonely and come home within a year. Under it: what would I do then? Find the gurdwara, help in the langar, phone home on Sundays, and if I still hated it, come back, no shame in that. Then: how likely? My cousin Harpreet was already there. Maybe not so likely. I read that page on the plane. The dread didn't vanish, but it had edges now.

qa.a: It came from the Toronto hospital accounts office.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as she lay awake, and why?
qa.a: She was frightened of being lonely and of the shame of coming back, so the excitement everyone else felt was swamped by dread.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Gurleen faced the move?
qa.a: Writing the feared outcome, then what she would do and how likely it was, gave her a plan, so the dread 'had edges' and she could get on the plane.

qa.a: She probably saw a daughter frightened under all the clapping, and chose to give her a way to think it through rather than just saying not to worry.

grounding: An elder recalls writing down her feared outcome, what she would do about it and how likely it was, which turned dread into options.

passage: In the government school at Palampur, the list for the Republic Day skit was pinned beside the water tank. Vidya read it twice. Her name wasn't there. On the walk home past the tea gardens she kicked every stone. 'Madam thinks I'm useless,' she told Tenzin. 'She thinks I can't even say two lines.' Tenzin shifted her schoolbag. 'Did she say that?' 'She doesn't need to. She never looks at me in class. She gave the queen's part to Kiran because Kiran is clever and I'm not.' 'Madam asked you to paint the backdrop last year,' Tenzin said. Vidya walked faster. 'That's different. That's just painting.'

qa.q: Where was the skit list pinned?
qa.a: It was pinned beside the water tank.

qa.q: Why did Vidya feel so sure Madam thought she was useless?
qa.a: She was hurt and disappointed at being left off the list, and that sting made her guess about Madam's thoughts feel like something she simply knew.

qa.q: What could Vidya do to check her belief?
qa.a: She could ask Madam how the parts were chosen, or remember facts like being asked to paint the backdrop, before deciding what Madam thinks.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Vidya's certainty?
qa.a: Tenzin doubts it, asking whether Madam actually said so and pointing to the backdrop, because she sees no real evidence.

grounding: A child not chosen for a skit states as fact that the teacher thinks she is useless, with no evidence.

passage: The class play parts went up on the board in Oslo on Tuesday afternoon, just before the bell. Wei got the troll. Ingrid got nothing: her name was under 'stage crew', with four others. On the tram home, she pressed her mitten against the fogged window. 'Mrs Halvorsen thinks I'm no good at anything,' she told her father. 'She thinks I'm boring and I'd ruin it.' Her father looked up from his phone. 'She said that?' 'She didn't have to. I could tell by her face when she read the list.' 'What was her face doing?' Ingrid frowned. She tried to remember, and couldn't. 'It was just... a face,' she said at last, more quietly.

qa.q: Which part did Wei get?
qa.a: Wei got the troll.

qa.q: What was Ingrid feeling on the tram, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was hurt and let down, pressing her mitten to the window, and that hurt made her guess about Mrs Halvorsen's thoughts feel certain.

qa.q: Why was her father's question about the teacher's face useful?
qa.a: It asked for real evidence, and when Ingrid couldn't remember any, she began to see her belief was a guess.

qa.q: How might Mrs Halvorsen explain the stage crew list?
qa.a: She might have reasons nobody on the tram knows, like needing reliable helpers backstage, which is why a guess about her thoughts can easily be wrong.

grounding: A child left off the cast list states as fact that the teacher thinks she is no good, based only on an imagined look.

passage: After evening study in the girls' hostel, Reena sat on her bunk with her knees pulled up. The annual day list had come out that afternoon, and Sangeeta Ma'am had not picked her for the dance drama. 'Sangeeta Ma'am thinks I'm useless,' she announced. 'She always has. She only picks the city girls.' Her bunkmate looked up from a geography map. 'She picked Lalitha, and Lalitha is from Karur.' 'That's one,' said Reena. 'Anyway, I saw how she looked at me in rehearsal. Like I was wasting her time.' She pulled the blanket over her head. When the warden came round for lights out, she stopped at Reena's bunk. 'Everything all right, kanna?' Reena said nothing, but she didn't pull her foot away when the warden patted it.

qa.q: Who did the bunkmate say was picked even though she is from Karur?
qa.a: The bunkmate said Lalitha was picked, and Lalitha is from Karur.

qa.q: Why did Reena state Sangeeta Ma'am's thoughts as if they were facts?
qa.a: She was hurt and embarrassed at not being picked, so one look in rehearsal felt like proof and she didn't stop to check it.

qa.q: How could the warden help Reena test her belief?
qa.a: The warden could listen, then ask what Sangeeta Ma'am actually said and encourage Reena to ask how the dancers were chosen.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta Ma'am feel if she knew what Reena believed?
qa.a: She might be surprised and sorry, since a look in rehearsal can mean tiredness or concentration rather than a judgement about Reena.

grounding: A child not chosen for the dance drama declares that the teacher thinks she is useless, treating a look as proof.

passage: Okay, Suraj, you asked why I left the school fest early, so here's the whole embarrassing thing. I'd worn my cousin's old kurta because nothing else was ironed. It was a bit loose, a bit faded. I walked into the auditorium and two girls in the third row put their heads together and whispered. I knew. I actually knew. They were saying, 'Look at Payal, did she come in her pyjamas?' I could hear it in my head like they'd said it into a mic. So I sat through two songs with my arms crossed over the kurta and then told the class teacher I had a headache. Yesterday one of those girls came up to me at the canteen. Guess what they'd been whispering about? Whether the principal had dyed his moustache. That's it. That's the whole story. I left a fest because of a moustache.

qa.q: What were the two girls actually whispering about?
qa.a: They were whispering about whether the principal had dyed his moustache.

qa.q: Why did Payal feel so certain the girls were mocking the kurta?
qa.a: Payal already felt self-conscious in a loose, faded kurta, so the whisper seemed to carry those exact words, and the imagined sentence felt as real as if it had been said into a mic.

qa.q: What could Payal try next time before leaving?
qa.a: Payal could notice the thought is only a guess, list other things people whisper about, or ask a friend to check, instead of acting on imagined words.

qa.q: What would change if Payal had known the real whisper that day?
qa.a: Payal might have laughed along about the moustache and stayed for the fest instead of sitting with crossed arms and leaving early.

grounding: A teenager sees two classmates whispering and treats imagined mockery of the kurta as words actually spoken, without checking.

passage:
Monday. Bhavna wore her sister's old maroon sweater to school because hers had shrunk. At the gate, Parveen leaned in and whispered something to Nisha, and both of them glanced at her. They're laughing at the sweater, Bhavna thought, and her face went hot. She kept her blazer buttoned all day.
Wednesday. She saw them whisper again near the library and walked the long way round to class. She didn't need to hear it. She knew what they were saying.
Friday. Parveen caught her at the water cooler. 'Where did you get that sweater? Nisha and I have been dying to ask. The cable pattern is so nice.' Bhavna stared. 'My sister's,' she said slowly. 'My grandmother knitted it.' All week, she realised, she had been answering a question nobody had asked.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna wear her sister's sweater?
qa.a: Bhavna wore it because her own sweater had shrunk.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna feel she knew the whisper without hearing it?
qa.a: She was already self-conscious about the old sweater, so her embarrassment filled in the words, and her imagined version felt as solid as real speech.

qa.q: What small step on Monday could have spared Bhavna the week?
qa.a: She could have noticed she hadn't heard a single word and treated her guess as a guess, or simply smiled and asked Parveen what was up.

qa.q: How did Parveen and Nisha see the sweater?
qa.a: They admired it and were keen to ask about the cable pattern, the opposite of what Bhavna imagined.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager treats classmates' whispers as mockery of her clothes without checking, until the truth turns out to be admiration.

passage: Lavanya, you say the whole class laughs at your shoes. Let your Lalit Mama tell you about a shirt. I was fourteen when we moved to Chennai from Thanjavur. Appa's old shirt was taken in by the tailor for my first day, and the collar still flapped. At the notice board, two boys looked my way and burst out laughing. That was it for me. I knew the words: village boy in his father's shirt. For a whole term I didn't raise my hand, didn't go near them, ate lunch by the tap. Then one of them, Srinivasan, found me by that tap. He needed a fourth for the quiz team. I asked him straight out what they had laughed at on my first day. He had to think hard. 'Oh! The cartoon of the headmaster in the paper!' One whole term, I had spent listening to a voice that was only mine.

qa.q: What did Srinivasan need when he found Lalit by the tap?
qa.a: He needed a fourth for the quiz team.

qa.q: Why was Lalit so sure the boys were laughing at his shirt?
qa.a: He felt out of place and self-conscious in his father's altered shirt, so their laugh seemed to carry exactly the words he feared, and the guess felt like a heard sentence.

qa.q: What turning point in the story broke the spell, and why?
qa.a: Asking Srinivasan straight out what they had laughed at replaced a term of guessing with the real answer, a cartoon of the headmaster.

qa.q: How did Srinivasan remember that first day?
qa.a: He barely remembered it and had to think hard; for him it was a laugh at a cartoon, not at Lalit at all.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a teenager, he was certain two laughing boys were mocking his shirt and treated the imagined words as spoken.

passage: Lakshmi had come off the night bus from Chennai at five, and by eleven she was sitting on the thinnai of Lalit's house in Kumbakonam while he laid out the plan for the temple fair: giant wheel first, then the bangle stalls, then the drama at nine. She nodded and rubbed her eyes. 'You clearly hate it,' Lalit said, folding the paper. 'Just say so. You always go quiet when you don't like something.' Lakshmi felt the words land wrongly, like being handed someone else's slippers. She wanted to snap back. Instead she took a breath. 'I don't hate it. I slept about two hours on that bus and my brain is soup. The wheel sounds fun. Can I sleep till four and meet you at the gate?' Lalit's face softened. 'Four. I'll save you a bangle stall.'

qa.q: When had Lakshmi got off the night bus?
qa.a: She had come off the night bus from Chennai at five.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi feel when Lalit said she clearly hated the plan?
qa.a: She felt misread and a bit irritated, like being handed someone else's slippers, and had to take a breath instead of snapping.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi's reply get right?
qa.a: She named her real state, tiredness, said what she liked, and offered a new time, which corrected the guess without starting a fight.

qa.q: Why might Lalit have read her silence as dislike?
qa.a: Lalit had seen her go quiet before when she disliked something, so he filled the silence with that old pattern instead of asking.

grounding: A tired friend is told she clearly hates the plan, feels misread, and gently says what she is actually feeling.

passage: Layla got back to the flat in Manchester at half past midnight, still smelling of coffee from the late shift. Selin was waiting at the kitchen table with a map of the Lake District spread out and three train times circled. 'Saturday, early train, hike to the tarn, fish and chips after,' she said. Layla sat down and stared at the circles. She couldn't think of a single word. Selin's smile dropped. 'Right. You obviously think it's a rubbish idea. You could just tell me instead of sulking.' Layla felt a flash of heat. I'm not sulking, I'm empty. She rubbed her face. 'Selin, I'm not against it. I've been on my feet for nine hours. Can you tell me again tomorrow, after I've slept? I want to hear it properly.' Selin looked at the map, then nodded and put the kettle on.

qa.q: How long had Layla been on her feet?
qa.a: She had been on her feet for nine hours.

qa.q: What was Layla feeling when Selin said she was sulking?
qa.a: She felt a flash of hurt and irritation at being misread, since she was simply exhausted and empty, not against the plan.

qa.q: What did Layla do that helped repair the moment?
qa.a: She named her real state, said she wasn't against the plan, and asked to hear it properly after sleep.

qa.q: Why might Selin have jumped to 'rubbish idea'?
qa.a: Selin had put effort into the map and train times and was likely eager and a little anxious, so silence felt like rejection.

grounding: A friend exhausted after a shift is told she thinks the plan is rubbish, feels misread, and gently explains what she is really feeling.

passage: The NSS committee met in Seminar Room 2 at eight in the morning, and Himani had submitted her chemistry lab record at three. She sat at the end of the table with her chin in her hand while Madhav sketched the plan for the lake clean-up on the whiteboard: gloves from the municipal office, forty volunteers, two buses. When he asked for comments, she said nothing. 'Himani obviously hates it,' Madhav said to the room, not unkindly but loudly. 'She'll tell us after the meeting that it won't work.' A couple of people laughed. Himani sat up. Her cheeks felt warm. 'I don't hate it,' she said evenly. 'I'm just exhausted. I finished a lab record at three. The plan looks good; I'd only add a water station.' Madhav wrote 'water station' on the board and underlined it.

qa.q: At what time did Himani submit her lab record?
qa.a: She had submitted her chemistry lab record at three.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when Madhav told the room she hated the plan?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and misjudged, her cheeks warm as people laughed, because her quiet came from exhaustion, not dislike.

qa.q: What made Himani's response work?
qa.a: She spoke evenly, named her real reason, praised the plan and added a useful idea, which corrected the guess without attacking Madhav.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel after hearing Himani's answer?
qa.a: He probably felt a little sheepish at having guessed wrong in front of the room, and showed he'd listened by underlining her idea.

grounding: In a committee meeting, a tired student is told she obviously hates the plan, feels misread, and calmly states her real feeling.

passage: Last month I spent most of a Wednesday convinced Abhinav was furious with me. He'd replied to my design draft with one word, 'Noted', no smiley, nothing, when he usually writes paragraphs. By lunch I had the whole conversation written in my head: he thought I'd ignored his notes, he'd complain to our lead, I'd defend myself, he'd say I always do this. I rehearsed my side on the metro home and again while cooking. The next morning I walked to his desk before I could chicken out. 'Hey, that "Noted" yesterday. Is something wrong with the draft, or with me?' He looked blank for a second, then laughed. 'Lavanya, my kid had a fever. I was typing with one thumb in the clinic queue. The draft's fine.' It took two minutes. I had spent about nine hours writing a fight neither of us was having.

qa.q: What one word did Abhinav reply with?
qa.a: He replied with one word, 'Noted'.

qa.q: Why did the imagined argument feel so convincing to Lavanya?
qa.a: Lavanya was anxious because 'Noted' was so unlike Abhinav's usual paragraphs, so the short reply felt like proof, and each rehearsal made the made-up fight feel more real.

qa.q: What made Lavanya's question effective?
qa.a: It was direct and offered two options, the draft or the relationship, so Abhinav could explain quickly, and two minutes replaced nine hours of guessing.

qa.q: What was the one-word reply like from Abhinav's side?
qa.a: For Abhinav it was just a quick note typed with one thumb in a clinic queue while worried about his child; there was no anger behind it.

grounding: An adult sure a colleague is annoyed asks him directly and learns the simple reason, replacing hours of imagined argument.

passage:
Mentoring notes, Thursday.
Chandrika came to our check-in looking as if she hadn't slept. She said Siddharth had been cold since she reorganised the shared tracker on Monday: short replies, no 'good morning', lunch at his desk. She had already drafted, in her head, the argument they would have, and an apology for things she wasn't sure she had done. I asked what she actually knew, as opposed to what she'd filled in. She counted: three short replies, one skipped lunch. I suggested one simple question, asked in person. She went straight after our meeting and was back in under five minutes. Siddharth had been on calls with his landlord all week about a leaking roof, and he liked the new tracker. Next step for me: a short session with her on checking before assuming, since this is the second time this month.

qa.q: What had Chandrika changed on Monday?
qa.a: She reorganised the shared tracker on Monday.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika feel so sure Siddharth was annoyed?
qa.a: She was anxious that her changes to the tracker had upset him, so short replies and a skipped lunch felt like proof, and she even prepared an apology for things she wasn't sure she'd done.

qa.q: What next step in the note would help Chandrika in future?
qa.a: The planned session on checking before assuming, plus listing what she knows versus what she has filled in, would help her ask sooner.

qa.q: How did the week look from Siddharth's side?
qa.a: Siddharth was busy with calls about a leaking roof and actually liked the new tracker, so his short replies had nothing to do with Chandrika.

grounding: A mentor's note shows an adult sure a colleague is annoyed checking directly, and a five-minute question ends days of imagined conflict.

passage:
Tuesday night
Writing this so I remember it. Since yesterday's review I'd been sure Suraj was annoyed with me. I presented the budget slides and he sat with his arms folded and didn't say a single thing. Last night I lay awake having the full argument: him saying I'd taken credit for his numbers, me saying I'd named him on slide two, him saying that wasn't enough. Round and round, till the fan's hum was all I could hear. Today at eleven I finally caught him at the printer. 'Suraj, are you upset about the review?' He blinked. 'Upset? I had a terrible headache. I could barely see the screen.' He even said the slides were clear. Two minutes by the printer, versus a whole night. Note to self, Seema: ask first, rehearse never.

qa.q: Where did Seema finally speak to Suraj?
qa.a: Seema caught him at the printer at eleven.

qa.q: What does Seema's sleepless night suggest about how the worry felt?
qa.a: Seema felt anxious and guilty, replaying the argument until only the fan's hum remained, because Suraj's folded arms seemed like a clear message.

qa.q: What habit does Seema take from this, and why is it useful?
qa.a: 'Ask first, rehearse never': a short direct question gives real information, while rehearsing only deepens a story built from guesses.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt during the review?
qa.a: Suraj was in pain and struggling to see the screen, so his folded arms and silence had nothing to do with Seema's slides.

grounding: An adult sure a colleague is annoyed asks directly, and a two-minute question replaces a night of imagined dialogue.
